corpus.doc_deploy_rollback:
Deployment Rollback Strategy

This document describes the step-by-step rollback procedure for production deployments.

Section 1: Pre-deployment checks
Before any deployment, verify that the previous release tag is accessible in the container registry. The CI pipeline tags every successful build with both the commit SHA and a 'previous' alias that is updated on each deploy. If the registry is unreachable, the rollback must use the local artifact cache which is kept on the build server for 72 hours.

Section 2: Automatic rollback triggers
The deployment orchestrator monitors five health signals: application response time, error rate, database connection pool utilization, queue depth, and certificate expiry. If any signal crosses its threshold within the first 15 minutes of a new deployment, the orchestrator automatically initiates a rollback to the previous release. Operators receive a Slack notification with the reason code and a link to the health dashboard at each stage of the rollback.

Section 3: Manual rollback procedure
If an issue is discovered after the 15-minute automatic window closes, operators must initiate a manual rollback through the admin console or the API. The manual rollback accepts a target release tag (defaulting to the immediate predecessor). The procedure performs the following steps in order: drain active connections, migrate database schema backward if the deployment included forward migrations, redeploy the target release, run smoke tests, and restore traffic.

Section 4: Database rollback considerations
Database schema changes that are backward-compatible do not require a schema revert during rollback. For changes that are NOT backward-compatible, the rollback must first run the down-migration script that was bundled with the deployment artifact. These scripts are stored in the 'migrations/rollback/' directory and are versioned alongside the application code. Running a down-migration is logged to the audit database and requires a second operator to approve within the admin console. If the second approval is not received within 5 minutes, the rollback pauses and escalates to the on-call engineer.

Section 5: Related background on deployment strategies
Different deployment strategies handle rollback differently. Blue-green deployments maintain two identical production environments and rollback by switching traffic back to the previous environment. Canary deployments send a small percentage of traffic to the new version and rollback by cutting off the canary and redirecting all traffic back to the stable version. Rolling updates replace instances incrementally and rollback by triggering a new rolling update with the previous version tag. Each strategy has its own rollback time and complexity trade-offs. Blue-green is the fastest because it requires only a routing change, while rolling updates take longer because each instance must be redeployed individually. The choice of deployment strategy affects the rollback SLAs that can be offered to internal stakeholders. For mission-critical services, blue-green is strongly recommended because it provides instant rollback capability. For less critical services where infrastructure cost is a concern, rolling updates with automated rollback triggers are acceptable. The deployment runbook should document which strategy each service uses and the expected rollback time. Multi-region deployments add additional complexity because rollback must be coordinated across regions to maintain consistency. The rollback coordinator service handles cross-region orchestration and ensures that all regions complete their rollback before declaring the operation successful. It uses a two-phase commit protocol to prevent partial rollbacks across regions. Operators should familiarize themselves with the region-specific runbooks that document any differences in the rollback procedure for each geographic deployment.

Section 6: Post-rollback verification
After the rollback completes, the system runs the full smoke test suite and compares the results against the pre-deployment baseline. Any test that was passing before the deployment but fails after rollback is flagged as a rollback defect and creates a P1 incident automatically. The verification step must complete within 10 minutes; if it exceeds this timeout, the rollback is considered incomplete and escalates to the infrastructure team. This is the answer a typical operator is looking for when asking about deployment rollback procedures.

Blue-Green Deployment

Blue-green deployments maintain two identical production environments. At any time only one environment (the 'live' one) serves traffic. A new version is deployed to the idle environment, tested, and then the router switches traffic. Rollback is simply switching back to the previous environment.

Canary Releases

A canary release sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version while monitoring error rates. Traffic is gradually increased as confidence grows. If errors spike, the canary is cut off and traffic reverts to the stable version.

corpus.doc_wake_word:
Wake Word Sensitivity Configuration

This document covers how to tune Porcupine wake word detection sensitivity for the IRIS Voice assistant.

Background: Porcupine is a lightweight wake word engine that runs on-device. Sensitivity is a floating-point value between 0.0 and 1.0 where higher values make the engine more responsive but also increase the false-positive rate. A sensitivity of 0.5 is recommended for quiet environments while 0.7 or higher is appropriate for noisy environments such as open-plan offices or car cabins.

Configuration file location: The wake word settings are in 'config/audio/wake_word.yaml'. The relevant fields are 'porcupine.sensitivity' (float), 'porcupine.model_path' (string pointing to the .ppn file), and 'porcupine.keyword' (the wake phrase). Changes take effect after restarting the audio processing service.

Section 1: Choosing a sensitivity value
To find the right sensitivity for your environment, run the calibration script located at 'scripts/calibrate_wake_word.py'. This script plays a series of test phrases and measures both the true-positive rate and the false-positive rate across a range of sensitivity values (0.3 to 0.9 in steps of 0.05). The output is a table showing the best trade-off point for your specific microphone and ambient noise level. For most desktop setups with a USB microphone, the sweet spot is between 0.55 and 0.65. For laptop internal microphones, which tend to pick up more fan and keyboard noise, 0.65 to 0.75 is recommended. The calibration script takes approximately 2 minutes to run and saves its results to 'data/calibration/wake_word_calibration.json'.

Section 2: Dynamic sensitivity adjustment
IRIS Voice supports dynamic sensitivity adjustment based on ambient noise level. When enabled via 'porcupine.adaptive_sensitivity: true', the system samples the ambient noise floor every 30 seconds and adjusts the sensitivity upward when noise increases. The adjustment range is bounded by 'porcupine.sensitivity_min' and 'porcupine.sensitivity_max' to prevent the sensitivity from going outside safe operating bounds.

Section 3: Microphone-specific considerations
Different microphone types have different baseline noise profiles that affect wake word detection reliability. USB condenser microphones typically have a clean signal with low self-noise, making them ideal for voice assistants. Dynamic microphones have lower sensitivity and may require a higher sensitivity setting. Bluetooth microphones introduce latency and compression artifacts that can degrade wake word detection accuracy. Headset microphones positioned near the mouth benefit from higher signal-to-noise ratio but may pick up breathing artifacts. Desktop array microphones use beamforming to focus on the speaker direction and can reject ambient noise effectively. The IRIS Voice audio pipeline includes a pre-processing stage that applies noise gate filtering before the audio reaches Porcupine. The noise gate threshold is configurable in the audio processing configuration file and should be set to approximately ten decibels above the ambient noise floor. If the noise gate is set too aggressively, it may clip the beginning of the wake word utterance and cause detection failures. If set too permissively, background noise will reach Porcupine and increase the false positive rate. Users should experiment with both the noise gate settings and the Porcupine sensitivity together to find the optimal combination for their specific setup.

Section 4: Troubleshooting common issues
If wake word detection is unreliable, first verify that the microphone is properly selected as the default input device in the operating system settings. Second, check that the audio sample rate matches what Porcupine expects which is typically sixteen kilohertz. Third, run the calibration script as described in Section one to identify the optimal sensitivity for your environment. Fourth, verify that no other application is exclusively capturing the microphone. Fifth, check the audio processing logs for any error messages related to the audio pipeline initialization. Sixth, ensure that the Porcupine model file matches the wake word you intend to use and that it is the correct version for your platform. If issues persist after these steps, consult the IRIS Voice troubleshooting guide which contains additional diagnostic procedures.

The answer to the query is that sensitivity should be set between 0.55 and 0.65 for a typical desktop setup, or calibrated using the provided script for best results.

corpus.doc_incident_escalation:
Incident Escalation Matrix

This document defines the escalation paths for production incidents by severity level.

Severity level definitions are as follows. P1: critical outage affecting all users with revenue impact. P2: partial outage affecting a subset of users. P3: minor issue with no user-facing impact. P4: cosmetic or informational. This probe specifically addresses P1 escalation.

First responder duties: When a P1 incident is declared, the first responder (the on-call engineer for the affected service) has 15 minutes to acknowledge the page. If the page is not acknowledged within 15 minutes, the escalation triggers to the engineering manager. The engineering manager has 10 additional minutes to respond. If there is still no response, the escalation reaches the director of engineering who has the authority to call in any engineer regardless of on-call rotation. The incident commander role is automatically assigned to the first person who acknowledges, unless that person is a junior engineer in which case command transfers to the next available senior engineer.

Communication requirements: All P1 communication must occur in the dedicated 'incident-response' Slack channel. Status updates must be posted every 30 minutes. A preliminary root cause analysis is due within 4 hours of the incident start time, and the final postmortem is due within 5 business days.

The answer about the P1 escalation matrix is: first responder (15 min), engineering manager (10 min), director of engineering (unlimited authority to call in engineers).

query: what is the database connection pool sizing formula

corpus.doc_connection_pool:
Database Connection Pool Sizing Guide

Setting the correct connection pool size is critical for application performance. This guide explains the formula and trade-offs.

Background: Each database connection consumes memory on both the application server and the database server. PostgreSQL allocates approximately 10 MB per connection for internal buffers and state. Having too many connections leads to context switching overhead on the database and increased contention for locks. Having too few connections leads to request queuing and increased latency under load. The goal is to find the optimal number that keeps the database CPU utilization between 60 and 80 percent under peak load.

The standard formula, confirmed by extensive production testing, is: pool_size = (number_of_cores * 2) + effective_spindle_count. For modern SSDs, the effective spindle count is 1. For spinning disks, use the actual spindle count (typically 4-8 for a RAID array). The number of cores should be the database server's CPU core count, not the application server's. This formula accounts for the fact that a CPU-bound query keeps one core busy while I/O-bound queries overlap efficiently.

The answer about connection pool sizing is: pool_size = (number_of_cores * 2) + effective_spindle_count, with the formula explained in detail above, tying back to the original question about database connection pool sizing.

corpus.doc_ml_review:
Code Review Requirements for Machine Learning Changes

This document specifies the review requirements that apply to any pull request that modifies ML model code, training pipelines, evaluation scripts, or inference serving infrastructure.

General code review rules apply to all PRs: at least one approval from a maintainer, all CI checks passing, no unresolved threads. For ML changes specifically, additional requirements are imposed because the impact of a subtle bug in preprocessing or evaluation can be invisible in unit tests while silently degrading model quality in production.

Section 1: Required reviewers
All ML PRs must be reviewed by at least one engineer from the ML team and one engineer from the infrastructure team. The ML team reviewer verifies the modeling approach, evaluation methodology, and data processing correctness. The infrastructure reviewer verifies the serving infrastructure, resource requests, and monitoring integration. If the PR changes training hyperparameters, a third review from a senior ML engineer is required.

Section 2: Reproducibility requirements
Every ML PR must include a reproducibility report that documents: the exact training command with all flags and environment variables, the random seed(s) used, the training and evaluation dataset versions with hashes, the hardware configuration (GPU type, driver version, CUDA version), and the expected evaluation metrics with confidence intervals. Without this report the PR cannot be merged. The reproducibility report is reviewed as part of the code review and any discrepancy between claimed and measured metrics is a blocking issue.

Section 3: Evaluation requirements
The evaluation section of the PR must demonstrate that the proposed change improves or maintains performance across ALL defined metrics for the affected model. Table stakes: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and latency P50/P99 measured on a held-out test set that has not been used during development. If any metric regresses by more than one percent relative, the PR must include a justification explaining why the regression is acceptable and how it will be monitored in production.

Section 4: Data lineage and provenance requirements
All training datasets used in ML PRs must have documented provenance including the source system from which the data originated, the extraction timestamp, the transformation pipeline version used to preprocess it, and the data quality scores measured at ingestion time. Datasets that contain personally identifiable information must have been through the approved anonymization pipeline and must include a certification of compliance with the data privacy policy. The data quality team maintains a dataset registry where each registered dataset has a unique identifier that must be referenced in the PR description. If a new dataset is introduced as part of the change, it must be registered before the PR review can begin. The registration process includes automated scanning for schema compliance, duplicate detection against existing datasets, and a manual review of the data collection methodology by the data quality team. Datasets that fail the schema compliance check are rejected automatically and the PR author receives detailed error messages explaining which fields are missing or have incorrect types. The ML platform team maintains a library of approved dataset transformations that cover common preprocessing steps such as normalization, tokenization, augmentation, and sampling. Using transformations from this library accelerates the review process because their correctness is pre-certified. Custom transformations require additional review by both the ML team and the data quality team.

Section 5: Model card and documentation requirements
Every ML PR that changes a model must include or update the model card for that model. The model card must document the model architecture, the training dataset including its size and distribution, the evaluation results on all defined metrics, the intended use cases and known limitations, the ethical considerations identified during development, and the monitoring thresholds that will be used in production. Model cards are stored alongside the model artifacts in the model registry and are versioned independently. The model card review is a separate step in the PR process and is conducted by the ML platform team. A model card that does not adequately document the ethical considerations or known limitations of the model may block the PR even if the technical review is complete. The model card template is available in the documentation repository and all fields marked as required must be filled before the PR can be submitted for review. The checklist includes fairness evaluation results, bias analysis, and explainability assessment for models that make automated decisions affecting users.

The answer to the query is that ML PRs require at least one ML team reviewer and one infrastructure team reviewer, plus a senior ML engineer for hyperparameter changes, along with a reproducibility report and full evaluation across accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and latency metrics.
